From behind the blind a voice came, soothing me, and I bowed in answer.

Maidono-no-Miya Haruhiro-shinnou, abbot of Hachimangu: this was my third audience with him. A man of such lofty standing, and such easy talk. The two do not match, strictly speaking, but by now I was no longer thrown by it.

Already a week and more had passed since the Enoshima business. Wounds and fatigue were nearly healed (Nikkari's visit had set me back a little, I admit), so nothing prevented me from showing His Highness proper courtesy.

I do not think that had been anyone's worry. Even so, the Chief, who had been watching me closely, now took his eyes off me and turned toward the prince's seat. Like a man asking leave, he spoke one word.

I clenched my back teeth and forced both eyes wide. For showing such an impossible disgrace, I turned on myself all the malice I had.

Tired? Nonsense. Am I a man who gets to sit soaking in such pleasures?

The people I had thrown with these hands into a state where they cannot even feel tiredness: what apology do I make to them? With what thickness of face did I let out such a weak word?

Unbelievable. And pitiful.

...Or is it only this, that I have already started to rattle? That I cannot hold up the bluff much longer?

—And just like that, I was playing with soft thoughts again.

Chief"...There lies the key. Whichever government of Yamato it may be, it needs the court's support when it establishes its rule. Without fail."
Chief"For a government that has already established its rule, the court is a portable shrine whose work is over. After that, so that nobody else uses it, it should sit quietly inside the godown. That is all."
Chief"But a government that is going to establish its rule cannot let the shrine sleep in the godown. It must carry the shrine out, parade it around the streets, and by its radiance make the people bow their heads."
Kageaki"...Then if that shrine has a will of its own, and wants of its own—"
Chief"Exactly. One who depends on the shrine cannot very well stay deaf to it, can he?"
Kageaki"...So that is why the king must be taken."
Chief"At present Rokuhara's rule is firm. But if it were made to lose the apex of that rule..."
Chief"The Rokuhara shogunate is held together, to a large degree, by the iron arm of one outstanding man, Moriuji Ashikaga. Whoever stands as his heir will need time to show the same arm."
Chief"Which means, naturally, many things will slip out of his hands."

en.html:
A fortress structure.

Shrines and temples are the refuge of the heart for the people of a place. For that reason, in older days, defenses were sometimes installed in them so that they could serve as strongholds in place of a castle, in times of war.

Nikko Toshogu may be the best example. That shrine, famous for its Yomeimon gate, is said in one account to have been also the Tokugawa family's final stronghold, in case it fell into trouble and had to retreat from Edo Castle.

As Toshogu was the Tokugawa clan's guardian, Hachimangu is the Minamoto clan's tutelary shrine. If it had the underground works that fortresses everywhere have as standard, perhaps there was no reason to be surprised.
